modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you go to one gathering where you will probably be the odd one out, such as a chess club in the park, a language exchange or a community garden day, and talk with at least two people you would not normally meet. You listen more than you explain and ask about their lives. Over time you return to the places where you felt welcome.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose social life has become narrow or repetitive, or who live mostly among people just like them. It may also suit anyone curious about other lives who wants to feel more at home in the wider community.
modalities.cautions: Choose groups that welcome newcomers and are respectful to everyone, and leave any setting that turns hostile or unsafe. If walking into unfamiliar groups brings intense anxiety, start with a friend or talk to a professional about it.
modalities.tweet: Most of us spend our time with people a lot like us. People Unlike Me, an untested habit: once a week, join one gathering where you are the odd one out, a chess club, a language exchange, a garden day, and meet two new people.

modalities.name: Side-by-Side Chores
modalities.tagline: Do your ordinary errands and chores together, unplanned and unreviewed.
modalities.whatItIs: Side-by-Side Chores is a new concept for folding friendship into ordinary life: instead of booking a special meetup, two to four friends do their errands and chores together, such as the weekly shop, the laundrette or a trip to the hardware store. Nothing is planned beyond meeting, and nobody reviews how it went.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT sets agendas, tests predictions and reviews progress; this is company with no structure, no self-monitoring and an accepting attitude, woven into whatever needs doing anyway. Being together matters more than what gets done.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you message a friend or two with whatever you have to do, such as buying groceries or returning a parcel, and whoever is free comes along with their own errands. You chat in the queue, help carry bags, swap opinions in the shop and stop for a drink if you feel like it, with no agenda. Afterward you skip the mental replay of what you said.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose social life has been squeezed out by chores and who over-plan or over-think their meetups. It could also work for busy parents and carers who cannot find time for separate social plans.
modalities.cautions: Choose company you feel safe and easy with, and step back from people who leave you feeling worse. If social worries or low mood persist despite good company, talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: No time for friends because of all the errands? Side-by-Side Chores, a new idea: do the weekly shop, the laundrette run or the hardware trip together, chatting as you go, with no plan and no post-mortem.

modalities.name: Tiny Wins Parties
modalities.tagline: Friends make a lively fuss over each other's small, ordinary wins.
modalities.whatItIs: Tiny Wins Parties is a new concept for making a lively fuss, together, over small and ordinary successes: a finished tax form, a first run, a hard conversation finally had. Friends cheer each other's wins whenever they meet, and once a month they throw a small party to celebrate all of them.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT works through metaphors and planned steps with a therapist; the opposite here is plain, unguided action in company, where people simply gather and cheer. Turning small steps into shared occasions is the whole idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Whenever you are with friends, at a dinner, after a class or on a doorstep, anyone can announce a tiny win, and the others cheer, raise whatever they are drinking and ask for the story. Once a month someone hosts a short party where everyone brings one win from the month and a snack to share. There are no speeches to prepare and no win is too small.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who brush off their own progress, or whose friendships only gather for big occasions. It could also suit anyone who would like more reasons to see friends.
modalities.cautions: Keep celebrations cheap and alcohol optional, and make sure the same few people do not always host or always get celebrated. If low mood makes every win feel pointless, that is worth raising with a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Finished your tax form? That deserves a cheer. In Tiny Wins Parties, a new concept, friends make a lively fuss over each other's small, ordinary wins whenever they meet, plus a little party each month for all of them.

modalities.name: Silly Outings Club
modalities.tagline: Friends meet to play like kids, with nothing serious allowed.
modalities.whatItIs: Silly Outings Club is a new concept for regular outings where a group of friends simply plays: swings, skimming stones, paddle boats, mini golf or a kite on a windy hill. Nothing serious is discussed and nothing has to be achieved; the play is the point.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy digs for the hidden emotional truths behind a problem; this keeps time together deliberately light and present, with no digging at all. Shared, silly play is valued in its own right.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a month three to eight friends pick somewhere playful, such as a park, a beach or a boating lake, and spend a couple of hours doing whatever looks fun, switching games whenever someone wants to. Phones stay in pockets apart from the odd photo, and if talk drifts to work or worries, someone suggests the next game. You finish with ice cream or a hot drink.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose friendships have turned into serious catch-ups about problems and who miss being silly together. It could also suit anyone who finds deep conversations draining but still wants close company.
modalities.cautions: Choose play that suits everyone's bodies and keep it gentle, and check the rules before adults use playground equipment. Light time together is no replacement for support when someone is struggling, so make room for that on another occasion.
modalities.tweet: When did you last skim stones with your friends? Silly Outings Club, an untested idea: a group meets to play, swings, paddle boats, mini golf, kites, and nothing serious is allowed.

modalities.name: Back-to-Back Calls
modalities.tagline: A lively run of voice calls, one after another, from your chair.
modalities.whatItIs: Back-to-Back Calls is an invented practice for a regular, lively round of voice calls with several different people, one after another. It is pure conversation: no video, no shared activity, nothing but voices, laughter and news.
modalities.coreIdea: TRE is physical, silent and done alone; this pushes socializing to the other extreme, with words only, many people and no body work at all. Talking is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three or four evenings a week you settle into a chair with a headset and call two or three people in a row, such as a sibling, an old friend and someone you have lost touch with, for 10 to 20 minutes each. You catch up, laugh, argue about films and swap news, letting each call run long or end early. If someone does not pick up, you leave a short, cheerful message and dial the next.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose friends and family are spread out, or who cannot easily get out in the evenings, and who want lively, regular contact. It might also appeal to anyone who talks more freely on the phone than face to face.
modalities.cautions: Keep calling the people who leave you feeling better rather than worse, and do not let calls crowd out sleep. If you find yourself calling to escape persistent low mood or loneliness, mention it to a doctor or therapist as well.
modalities.tweet: Remember long, lively phone calls? Back-to-Back Calls, a new concept: a few evenings a week, ring two or three people in a row, a sibling, an old friend, someone you lost touch with. Just voices, no video. 📞

modalities.name: Running Commentary Walks
modalities.tagline: Friends stroll through town, riffing out loud on everything they notice.
modalities.whatItIs: Running Commentary Walks is a new concept for lively group strolls through a busy town or market in which friends keep up a running, out-loud commentary on everything they notice: odd shop signs, overheard snippets, the best dog of the day. The talk is quick, playful and outward, and anyone can jump in.
modalities.coreIdea: Focusing waits slowly and quietly for something to form inside; this goes toward quick, outward, energetic talk with other people about what is right in front of you. Saying it out loud the moment you notice it, and riffing on what others say, is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three to six friends meet at a busy spot and wander for an hour or two at an easy stroll, pointing things out and building on each other's remarks, with no route and no destination. Someone might award a prize for the strangest sight or the best snippet, and the walk ends at a café where the best moments get retold. Comments stay kind about the people you pass.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who spend a lot of time inside their own heads and want lively, outward company. It could also suit friends who run out of things to say when they sit down together.
modalities.cautions: Keep remarks about passers-by kind and out of their earshot, and watch for traffic while you are busy talking. If social situations bring intense anxiety, start with one close friend.
modalities.tweet: The strangest shop sign, the best dog of the day, that overheard snippet: Running Commentary Walks is an untested idea where friends stroll through town riffing out loud on everything they notice. Quick, playful and outward.

modalities.name: The Favor Web
modalities.tagline: Ask neighbors and friends for small favors, and offer them back.
modalities.whatItIs: The Favor Web is an untested idea for deliberately weaving your social ties through small favors: asking a neighbor to lend you a ladder, offering to water someone's plants, swapping a lift for a home-cooked meal. Each favor creates a reason to talk again.
modalities.coreIdea: Aletheia Coaching slows down to let inner experience unfold; this goes toward brisk, practical action that changes your social world, done without any coach. Small acts of asking and giving become the threads of connection.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you ask one small, easy favor of someone nearby and offer one, such as borrowing a tool, sharing extra vegetables or carrying a parcel up the stairs. You return borrowed things promptly with a little thank-you, which often turns into a short chat. Over a few months you keep a rough sense of who helps whom and look for ways to even it out.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are reluctant to ask for help and have few ties in their street, building or workplace. It may also suit those who have just moved and want to become part of a neighborhood.
modalities.cautions: Keep favors small, easy to decline and evenly balanced over time, and never ask for anything that would put someone at risk or out of pocket. If asking for help feels impossible, that may be worth exploring with a therapist.
modalities.tweet: Asking a neighbor for a cup of sugar used to be normal. The Favor Web, a new idea: each week ask one small favor and offer one, a ladder, a lift, spare vegetables, and return things with a thank-you. Handy if you are new to the street.

modalities.name: Be the Convener
modalities.tagline: Start and host a small regular gathering yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Be the Convener is a new concept for taking charge of your social life by starting and hosting a small, regular gathering: a monthly dinner, a walking group, a book swap or a games night. Instead of waiting to be included, you create the occasion and invite people in.
modalities.coreIdea: Do Nothing meditation sets out to change nothing; this is the reverse, with initiative, a light structure and active change in who you see and how often. Being the one who brings people together is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a simple format you would enjoy, set a fixed day, such as the first Friday of each month, and invite five to ten people, asking each to bring someone new once in a while. You handle the small jobs: reminders, a place to meet and a welcome at the door. After three or four gatherings you adjust the format based on who keeps coming and why.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel left out or tired of waiting for invitations, and who like having a project. It might also appeal to those who are good at organizing but rarely use that skill for friendship.
modalities.cautions: Hosting can become a burden, so keep the format cheap and simple, share the tasks and pause when you need to. If hosting brings intense worry, or a thin turnout leaves you crushed, talk it over with someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: If nobody organizes it, it does not happen. Be the Convener, a proposal: pick a simple format, a monthly dinner, a walking group, a book swap, set a fixed day and invite five to ten people. You make the occasion.

modalities.name: Said Out Loud
modalities.tagline: Speak your appreciation to several people, face to face, every day.
modalities.whatItIs: Said Out Loud is a proposed habit of speaking your appreciation, admiration or affection aloud to several people every day, face to face, and at every gathering you go to. It turns kind thoughts into real, spoken moments with real people.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta cultivates goodwill silently, alone and toward people held in mind; this turns it into spoken words to real faces, with no set phrases. Saying it directly, while the feeling is fresh, is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each day you aim to tell at least three people something specific you appreciate about them, such as a colleague who handled a meeting well or a shopkeeper who always remembers your order, in a sentence or two. At dinners and parties you make a point of telling each person you talk with one thing you enjoyed about them before you leave. You keep it simple, honest and specific, for example that their help on Tuesday made a real difference.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel warmly toward others but rarely say so, and who would like their relationships to feel closer. It may also appeal to anyone who practices loving-kindness meditation and wants to take it off the cushion.
modalities.cautions: Keep it honest and suited to the relationship, especially at work, and do not expect anything in return. Some people find compliments awkward, so a light touch works better than a speech.
modalities.tweet: Thought something kind about someone and kept it to yourself? Said Out Loud, an untested habit: tell at least three people a day, face to face, one specific thing you appreciate about them.

modalities.name: The Talking Weekend
modalities.tagline: The opposite of a silent retreat: a weekend of nonstop conversation.
modalities.whatItIs: The Talking Weekend is a new concept for a self-organized weekend away with a group of friends where conversation is the whole point: long meals, late nights and endless talk, with no screens and no schedule. It is the deliberate opposite of a silent retreat.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana turns attention inward, alone and without speaking, often on silent retreats; this takes socializing the opposite way, toward lively, wordy, shared time. Plenty of unhurried talk among friends is the core of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight friends rent a cabin or borrow a house for two nights, agree to put phones away and arrive with nothing planned except meals. You cook, eat and talk for hours, about memories, ideas, plans and nonsense, letting conversations split into pairs and come back together. On the last morning each person names one conversation they will remember.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose friendships have shrunk to quick messages and short catch-ups and who want to reconnect properly. It could also interest anyone who has tried silent retreats and is curious about the opposite.
modalities.cautions: A weekend of nonstop company can be tiring, so anyone should feel free to slip away for quiet time, and alcohol stays optional. Choose people you trust, and if old conflicts are likely to flare, agree in advance how to step back.
modalities.tweet: Silent retreats are a thing. What about the opposite? The Talking Weekend: four to eight friends, one cabin, two nights, phones away, nothing planned but meals and hours of conversation. A new idea for friendships shrunk to texting.

modalities.name: Long Talk by the Embers
modalities.tagline: One slow, shared conversation around a fire, lasting all evening.
modalities.whatItIs: Long Talk by the Embers is an untested idea for unhurried evenings where a small group sits around a fire pit or wood stove and holds one long conversation together, the whole group in it at once. The pace is slow and easy, but talking and listening to each other is the whole activity.
modalities.coreIdea: HIIT is fast, hard and tightly timed; this is socializing slowed right down, with stillness, calm and no structure, but with everyone in the same conversation. Instead of splitting into pairs and small talk, the group keeps one thread going for hours.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight people settle around a fire as it gets dark, with blankets and hot drinks, and someone starts with an easy question, such as the best place they have ever slept. The conversation wanders from there at its own pace, with everyone free to add, ask or just listen, and side conversations are gently folded back into the main one. It ends when the fire burns down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find busy social events exhausting but still want real, sustained conversation with others, including anyone recovering from burnout. It could also suit friends who only ever meet in loud places.
modalities.cautions: Follow local rules on fires, keep water nearby and keep children and blankets away from the flames. Calm company is gentle, but loneliness or low mood that persists despite it is worth raising with a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: One fire, one long conversation, everyone in it. Long Talk by the Embers, an untested idea: a small group keeps a single slow conversation going until the fire burns down. The opposite of loud, busy socials.

modalities.name: Castles in the Air Club
modalities.tagline: Friends daydream out loud together about delightfully impossible plans.
modalities.whatItIs: Castles in the Air Club is a new concept for relaxed get-togethers where friends daydream out loud together about plans that will probably never happen: opening a café on a boat, cycling across a continent, building a treehouse village. Nobody competes, nobody wins and nothing needs to be realistic.
modalities.coreIdea: Team sport is physical, competitive and fast; this keeps the company but drops the contest, so people sit still and build ideas with each other instead of against each other. Shared imagination becomes the way people get to know each other.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every couple of weeks four to eight friends meet in someone's kitchen or a quiet pub corner, and whoever arrives with a daydream starts it off. The others add to it, ask what the café would serve or where the treehouses would go, and the dream grows or drifts into a new one, with no format and no time limit. Now and then a dream turns out to be doable, and someone writes it down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want close, playful company without competition, physical effort or heavy topics. It could also suit anyone who loves ideas and misses having people to dream with.
modalities.cautions: Keep it kind, with no mocking of anyone's dream, and money or life plans stay optional to discuss. If daydreaming starts to feel like a way of avoiding real problems, talk to someone you trust.
modalities.tweet: A café on a boat? A treehouse village? Castles in the Air Club, a new idea: friends meet to daydream out loud about wonderful, unlikely plans, building on each other's ideas, with nobody competing.

modalities.name: The Findable Regular
modalities.tagline: Be findable at one café corner each week, and let people join.
modalities.whatItIs: The Findable Regular is a new concept for staying put and letting company find you: at the same time each week you sit at the same corner of a local café or pub, and friends, neighbors and acquaintances know they can drop by. You do not host or organize; you are simply there.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance training means going out and covering distance under your own power; this does the reverse, staying in one place and letting people come to you. Being reliably findable, with almost no structure, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick a time, such as Saturday from ten to twelve, and a corner where staff will not mind you lingering, and tell a few people you will be there every week. You bring a book or a crossword, chat with whoever turns up, get to know the staff and other regulars and introduce people to each other. Some weeks the table fills and some weeks you read, and either way you come back the next week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who would like more company but find organizing events tiring or hosting at home impractical. It could also suit newcomers to an area who want to become a familiar face.
modalities.cautions: Choose a venue where lingering is welcome, buy something now and then and keep alcohol optional. If the weeks when nobody comes feel crushing, that is worth talking through with someone.
modalities.tweet: New concept: The Findable Regular. Same café corner, same time, every week, so everyone you know can find you there. No hosting, no planning, just being reliably around.

modalities.name: Advice-Free Gatherings
modalities.tagline: Friends meet to listen to each other, with one rule: no advice.
modalities.whatItIs: Advice-Free Gatherings is a new concept for regular meetups of friends with one simple rule: nobody gives advice or tries to solve anyone else's problems. You talk about what is going on in your lives, and the others listen, ask questions and keep you company.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training is about effort, progress and pushing to improve; this goes toward accepting each other as you are, with no improvement plans. Being heard without being managed is the heart of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight friends meet every couple of weeks over food or coffee for a couple of hours. When someone shares a struggle, the others respond with curiosity rather than suggestions, for example by asking what it has been like, and anyone can call 'advice alert' with a smile if the rule slips. If someone actually wants advice, they ask for it outright.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of getting unasked-for solutions from well-meaning friends, or who catch themselves giving advice instead of listening. It could also work for any friend group that wants to feel more supportive.
modalities.cautions: Listening is no substitute for professional help, so if someone shares something serious, such as thoughts of self-harm, the rule gives way and the group helps them get support. Keep the group small and every topic voluntary.
modalities.tweet: One rule: no advice. In Advice-Free Gatherings, an untested idea, four to eight friends meet every couple of weeks, share what is going on, and the others just listen and ask questions.

modalities.name: Seat Swap Feasts
modalities.tagline: A lively shared supper at one long table, strangers welcome.
modalities.whatItIs: Seat Swap Feasts is an invented format for lively, self-organized community meals where neighbors and strangers share one long table, talk and swap seats before dessert. There is no host on a stage, no program and no professional: just food, noise and conversation.
modalities.coreIdea: Animal-assisted therapy is calm, guided and often wordless; this pushes socializing the other way, to loud, chatty, unguided human company with nothing in between people. The long table puts everyone shoulder to shoulder with someone new.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a month a few volunteers borrow a hall, a courtyard or a closed-off street, push tables into one long line and invite anyone to bring a dish to share. You sit wherever there is space, introduce yourself to the people beside and across from you, and stay as long as you like, usually two or three hours. Seats change before dessert so everyone meets someone new.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a big, warm dose of human company and a way to meet people in their area. It may also suit anyone who finds one-to-one meetups intense but enjoys the buzz of a crowd.
modalities.cautions: Label dishes for common allergens, and keep the event open, alcohol optional and safe for everyone, including children and older guests. Noisy crowds can be overwhelming, so a quiet corner or an early exit should always be fine.
modalities.tweet: One long table, a dish each, neighbors and strangers side by side. Seat Swap Feasts, a new idea: monthly community meals with no program, just food, lively talk and a change of seats before dessert. 🍲

modalities.name: Into the Crowd
modalities.tagline: Seek out busy, buzzing public gatherings and join in.
modalities.whatItIs: Into the Crowd is a new concept for regularly joining lively public gatherings, such as street festivals, match screenings, parades and local celebrations, and sharing in the crowd's energy. The aim is to cheer, sing and clap along with hundreds of others, not to hold conversations.
modalities.coreIdea: Qigong is quiet, slow, mostly solitary and set in its form; this goes toward noise, spontaneity and the energy of many people at once. Shared excitement in a crowd is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a month you check local listings and go to one big public event, alone or with a friend, for an hour or two. You join in with whatever the crowd is doing, such as clapping along, cheering a goal, singing a chorus or waving along a parade route. You leave whenever you have had enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel flat, isolated or stuck at home and want a jolt of collective energy. It might also appeal to those who like being among people without the pressure of one-to-one conversation.
modalities.cautions: Crowds can be overwhelming or unsafe, so know your exits, drink water, keep alcohol moderate or skip it, and leave if things feel tense. If crowds bring on panic, start with smaller events and talk to a professional.
modalities.tweet: Feeling flat? Try a crowd. Into the Crowd, a new concept: once or twice a month, go to one big public event, a street festival, a match screening, a parade, and cheer, sing and clap along with everyone else. Leave whenever you like.

modalities.name: Make Something Together
modalities.tagline: Friends meet indoors to invent and make one shared project.
modalities.whatItIs: Make Something Together is a new concept for lively indoor sessions where a group of friends invents and makes one shared project over a few weeks, such as a zine, a short film, a board game of their own or a plan for a street party. The ideas, arguments and laughs along the way are the social heart of it.
modalities.coreIdea: Nature walks are open, outdoors and full of the senses; this brings socializing indoors, around a table, with a light plan and lots of lively, imaginative back-and-forth. A shared creation gives everyone a reason to keep meeting and talking.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight friends meet weekly for two or three hours at someone's kitchen table or a library room, pick a project together and split it into small jobs. Each session starts with a quick look at what got done, then people brainstorm, sketch, write or build, swapping roles as they go. When the project is finished you share it, celebrate and pick the next one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find unstructured socializing awkward, prefer having something to make together and enjoy ideas. It could also suit creative people whose hobbies are usually solitary.
modalities.cautions: Keep the project small enough to finish and the costs low, and make sure quieter members get a say. If disagreements turn sour, take a break or pick a simpler project.
modalities.tweet: A zine, a short film, a board game of your own: in Make Something Together, an untested idea, a group of friends meets weekly to invent and build one shared project.

modalities.name: Friendly Argument Club
modalities.tagline: Lively, good-humored debate about ideas, among friends who disagree.
modalities.whatItIs: Friendly Argument Club is a new concept for regular evenings where friends gather to argue, in good humor, about ideas, books, films or big questions. The aim is lively exchange and changing minds, your own included, rather than calm agreement.
modalities.coreIdea: Sensory mindfulness is quiet, solitary and rooted in the senses; this goes toward ideas, enthusiastic voices and active attempts to persuade. Disagreeing well, together, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to ten people meet every couple of weeks in a home or a pub back room, someone brings a question, such as whether cities should ban cars, and the group argues it out for an hour or two. Anyone can switch sides partway through, and the evening ends with everyone saying what, if anything, moved them. Insults are off limits, and laughing at a good point from the other side is encouraged.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love ideas, find polite small talk dull and want friends who will push back. It could also work for anyone who wants to practice disagreeing without falling out.
modalities.cautions: Avoid topics that touch someone's identity or recent pain unless everyone agrees to them, and stop if an argument turns personal or hostile. If conflict makes you very anxious, start as a listener.
modalities.tweet: Bored of polite small talk? Friendly Argument Club, a new concept: five to ten friends, one big question, an hour or two of good-humored debate, and anyone can switch sides. It ends with everyone saying what changed their mind.

modalities.name: Phones in the Basket
modalities.tagline: Gatherings with phones in a basket and no background music.
modalities.whatItIs: Phones in the Basket is a proposed practice for get-togethers where everyone drops their phone in a basket at the door and the music stays off, so nothing competes with the conversation. You hear each other properly, and attention stays on the faces in the room.
modalities.coreIdea: Music fills a room with sound and mood. This strips the background away and leaves plain, undistracted conversation with the people actually present.
modalities.whatYouDo: Whenever you host friends, for dinner, drinks or a lazy afternoon, you put a basket by the door, ask guests to leave their phones in it and keep the music off. The evening is just talk, food and whatever the group decides to do, with no screens and no soundtrack. Anyone can step out to check their phone if they need to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice that gatherings keep getting interrupted by screens or drowned out by music and want fuller conversations. It may also suit anyone with hearing difficulties, for whom background noise makes talk hard to follow.
modalities.cautions: Keep a way to be reached in emergencies, such as leaving ringers on in the basket, and never pressure someone who needs their phone for health, care or work reasons. A quiet room can feel awkward at first, so a game or a shared task can help break the ice.
modalities.tweet: No phones, no playlist, just the people in the room. Phones in the Basket, a new idea: phones go in a basket at the door, music stays off, and the conversation gets everyone's full attention.
